name: FUTURE
aliases: Female Urgency, Trial of Urodynamics as Routine Evaluation
question: Does adding invasive urodynamics to comprehensive clinical assessment improve patient-reported success before invasive treatment for refractory overactive bladder symptoms in women?

design.population: Women with refractory overactive bladder or urgency-predominant mixed urinary incontinence after unsuccessful conservative management and at least two pharmacological treatments unless contraindicated, considering invasive treatment.
design.locator: Full text, Methods and trial profile, pp 1058–1059

verdictNote: Added urodynamics did not improve final patient-reported success.
takeaway: In women considering invasive treatment for refractory overactive bladder symptoms, urodynamics plus comprehensive clinical assessment did not improve final patient-reported success versus comprehensive clinical assessment alone (23.6% versus 22.7%; adjusted OR 1.12, 95% CI 0.73–1.74).

delivery.value: Among 494 with a urodynamic diagnosis available: detrusor overactivity or detrusor overactivity incontinence 287/494 (58.1%); urodynamic stress incontinence 65/494 (13.2%); urodynamic mixed incontinence 39/494 (7.9%); neither stress incontinence nor detrusor overactivity confirmed 102/494 (20.6%). delivery.label: Urodynamic quality assurance
delivery.value: An expert panel reviewed 124 randomly selected traces or reports; it disagreed with the local diagnosis in 5/124 (4.0%), and these diagnoses were changed.

reports.citation: Abdel-Fattah M, Chapple C, Breeman S, et al. "Invasive urodynamic investigations in the management of women with refractory overactive bladder symptoms: FUTURE, a superiority RCT and economic evaluation." *Health Technol Assess.* 2025;29(27):1-139. doi:10.3310/UKYW4923
reports.followUp: Within-trial follow-up to 15 or 24 months; lifetime cost-effectiveness model

results.measure: Modelled lifetime NHS cost and QALYs per participant
results.note: Urodynamics was dominated: £1,380 higher cost and 0.002 fewer QALYs; 23.4% probability of cost-effectiveness at £20,000 per QALY. The model extrapolated beyond trial follow-up using external evidence; no confidence interval or P value was reported for this estimate.

results.measure: Estimated 24-month mean NHS cost per participant, multiple-imputation analysis
results.note: Within-trial analysis of all 1,099 participants with imputed missing data; ICER £42,643 per QALY gained and 33.82% probability of cost-effectiveness at £20,000 per QALY. Complete-case sensitivity analysis gave 67.26% probability at the same threshold. No P value was reported for the cost difference.
results.locator: Full text, Chapter 5, Tables 16 and 20, pp 48, 50

results.measure: Estimated 24-month QALYs per participant, multiple-imputation analysis
results.note: Within-trial analysis of all 1,099 participants with imputed missing data; no P value was reported for the QALY difference.

harms.label: Serious adverse events
harms.note: Five deaths were unrelated to trial participation; four expected serious events comprised an anaesthetic complication, hospitalised possible pyelonephritis/UTI, and two instances of self-catheterisation after botulinum toxin A. Arm-specific counts and Clavien-Dindo grades were not reported.
harms.locator: Full text, Chapter 4, Safety data, p 39
